The hierarchy

Four bit-addressed levels, from the atomic codepoint to the zone, all derived by bit-shifting.

  1. Zone — 128 zones (bits 24–30)
  2. District — 256 per zone (bits 16–23)
  3. Plane — 256 per district (bits 8–15)
  4. Offset — 256 codepoints (bits 0–7)
Level Span Derived by Notes
Codepoint 1 — The atomic unit; e.g. 0x0011A000
Offset 256 codepoints CP & 0xFF One plane
Plane 256 offsets CP >> 8 & 0xFF 65,536 codepoints
District 256 planes CP >> 16 & 0xFF 16,777,216 codepoints
Zone 256 districts CP >> 24 & 0x7F 4,294,967,296 codepoints — the top field
Block variable named run Not an address field. Recorded in Blocks.txt
Range variable declared allocation Not an address field. Plugins declare ranges; collisions are rejected at boot

The math

Address arithmetic makes the hierarchy total and cheap. 128 zones × 256 districts × 256 planes × 256 offsets = 231 exactly, so the four fields tile the codespace with no gaps. Take the start of the BANcode registry, 0x0011A000:

SUCS_CP 0x0011A000
plane 0x0011 >> 8 & 0xFF = 0xA0
district 0x0011 >> 16 & 0xFF = 0x11 // District 17
zone 0x0011 >> 24 & 0x7F = 0x00

Note that Block and Range are semantic groupings, not address levels. They are variable-length by design, and nothing in the bit arithmetic depends on them — which is exactly why they cannot be bit fields. See SUTR-0 §1.2 (source: docs/sutr/SUTR-0-sucs-core.md).
